final_note: You worked through Changes of state and the particle model — 16 specification statements.

concepts.def: Density is the mass of a material per unit volume. The specification defines it by the equation density = mass / volume. A material has a high density when a large mass is packed into a small volume. Density is a property of the material itself: it does not depend on how much of the material you have.

In words, density = mass / volume. In symbols, ρ = m/V, where ρ is the density, m is the mass and V is the volume. This is an equation students are expected to recall and apply, and to rearrange as m = ρV or V = m/ρ.

In the equation as the specification states it, density, ρ, is in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³. The unit follows directly from the equation: a mass in kilograms divided by a volume in metres cubed gives kilograms per metre cubed.
Mass, m, is in kilograms, kg. Mass is measured on a balance. Weight is a force measured in newtons and must not be substituted into ρ = m/V in place of mass.

Volume, V, is in metres cubed, m³. For a regularly shaped solid the volume is calculated from its measured dimensions (for a cuboid, length x width x height). For an irregularly shaped solid it is found by a displacement technique.

Densities are often quoted in g/cm³, but the specification's unit is kg/m³. Since 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, a density of 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³. To convert from g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000. Water is about 1.0 g/cm³, that is 1000 kg/m³.

A model that treats a substance as being made of atoms or molecules whose arrangement, separation and movement differ from one state of matter to another. The specification uses the particle model to explain the different states of matter and differences in density.
In a solid the particles are packed closely together, touching one another in a regular arrangement, and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid keeps its own shape and its own volume.
In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but they are arranged randomly and can move past one another. A liquid keeps its own volume but takes the shape of its container.

In a gas the particles are far apart compared with the size of the particles themselves, arranged randomly, and move quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume; it fills its container.

concepts.term: Simple particle diagrams of the three states
concepts.def: A solid is drawn as circles touching in a regular, ordered pattern. A liquid is drawn as circles touching but jumbled, filling the lower part of the container. A gas is drawn as a few widely separated circles spread through the whole container. The circles are the same size in all three diagrams, because the particles themselves do not change.

concepts.term: Explaining differences in density from the arrangement of particles
concepts.def: The particles of a given substance have the same mass in every state, so a difference in density must come from a difference in the volume the same particles occupy. Solids and liquids have similar densities because in both the particles are touching. A gas is very much less dense, commonly by a factor of about a thousand, because the same particles are spread through a far larger volume.

concepts.term: Determining the density of a regular solid
concepts.def: Measure the mass of the object on a balance. Measure its dimensions with appropriate apparatus and calculate the volume from those dimensions (for a cuboid, length x width x height). Then calculate density using ρ = m/V.

concepts.term: Displacement technique for an irregular solid
concepts.def: The volume of an irregularly shaped object is found by displacement. Lower the object, fully submerged, into a measuring cylinder holding a known volume of water and record the new reading; the volume of the object is the increase in the reading. Alternatively, lower it into a displacement can filled to the spout and measure the water that overflows in a measuring cylinder. Its mass is measured separately on a balance.

concepts.term: Determining the density of a liquid
concepts.def: Measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder on a balance. Pour the liquid in, record its volume, and measure the mass again. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two balance readings, and the density is that mass divided by the measured volume.

The specification names a ruler, a micrometer and Vernier callipers. The instrument is chosen to suit the size of the dimension being measured: a ruler (resolution about 1 mm) for a block a few centimetres across, Vernier callipers (about 0.1 mm) for smaller objects, and a micrometer (about 0.01 mm) for very small dimensions such as the diameter of a wire.

The specification names six changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating. Melting is solid to liquid and freezing is liquid to solid; boiling and evaporating are liquid to gas and condensing is gas to liquid; sublimating is solid straight to gas.

concepts.term: Conservation of mass in a change of state
concepts.def: When a substance changes state, mass is conserved: no particles are created or destroyed, so the mass after the change is equal to the mass before it. If a balance reading falls while a liquid boils away, the mass has left the container as a gas; it has not been destroyed.

A change of state is a physical change. It differs from a chemical change because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed. No new substance is produced; only the arrangement and the movement of the particles change.

mcqs.q: How is the density of a material defined?
options: The volume of the material divided by its mass.
The mass of the material multiplied by its volume.
The mass of the material, whatever its volume is.
The mass of the material divided by its volume.
mcqs.explain: This is the definition the specification gives: density = mass / volume, or ρ = m/V.

mcqs.q: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³ and a mass of 2.0 kg. What is its volume?
options: 400 m³
mcqs.explain: Rearranging ρ = m/V gives V = m/ρ = 2.0 / 800 = 0.0025 m³.

mcqs.q: Which unit does the specification use for density?
options: g/cm³
kg/m³
m³/kg
kg/m²
mcqs.explain: The specification states density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.

mcqs.q: A solid cube of side 0.20 m has a mass of 54 kg. What is its density?
options: 270 kg/m³
1350 kg/m³
0.43 kg/m³
6750 kg/m³

mcqs.q: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this in kg/m³?
options: 2700 kg/m³
2.7 kg/m³
27 kg/m³
mcqs.explain: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so 2.7 g/cm³ = 2.7 x 1000 = 2700 kg/m³.

mcqs.q: Which description matches a correct simple particle diagram of a solid?
options: Particles touching each other in a regular, ordered pattern.
Particles evenly spaced in a grid, with gaps in between them.
Particles touching one another but jumbled, not in a pattern.
Particles well spread out and moving quickly in all directions.
mcqs.explain: A solid is close-packed and ordered; both features must appear in the diagram.

mcqs.q: Why is the density of a gas far lower than the density of the same substance as a liquid?
options: The particles in a gas are lighter than those in a liquid.
The same particles are spread through a much larger volume.
Each particle grows bigger when the liquid becomes a gas.
The particles move faster, so gravity pulls on them less.
mcqs.explain: Mass per particle is unchanged, so the drop in density comes entirely from the increase in volume.

mcqs.q: A block of solid wax melts. The mass does not change, but the liquid wax takes up slightly more volume. What happens to the density?
options: It stays the same, because exactly the same particles are present.
It falls a long way, because liquid particles are far apart.
It falls slightly, because the particles are a little further apart.
It falls, because each particle becomes larger as the wax melts.
mcqs.explain: With m fixed and V slightly larger, ρ = m/V is slightly smaller. Solids and liquids have similar densities because the particles stay in contact.

mcqs.q: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?
options: The mass on a balance, and the area of its largest face.
The weight in newtons, and the length, width and height.
The mass on a balance, and the length, width and height.
The mass on a balance, and the length of its longest side.
mcqs.explain: The volume of a regularly shaped object is calculated from its dimensions, and the mass is measured on a balance.

mcqs.q: A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm³ of water. A stone of mass 60 g is lowered in and the level rises to 65 cm³. What is the density of the stone?
options: 0.92 g/cm³
1.5 g/cm³
0.42 g/cm³
2.4 g/cm³
mcqs.explain: The stone displaces 65 - 40 = 25 cm³ of water, so ρ = 60 / 25 = 2.4 g/cm³.

mcqs.q: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 85 g. It is filled to the 50 cm³ mark with oil and the total mass is 129 g. What is the density of the oil?
options: 2.58 g/cm³
1.14 g/cm³
0.88 g/cm³
1.70 g/cm³
mcqs.explain: The oil alone has a mass of 129 - 85 = 44 g, so ρ = 44 / 50 = 0.88 g/cm³.

mcqs.q: Which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?
options: A micrometer, which has a resolution of about 0.01 mm.
A ruler, because 0.4 mm can be judged between the marks.
Any of the three, since they all measure a length in mm.
Vernier callipers, which read to the nearest millimetre.
mcqs.explain: The resolution is far smaller than the diameter, so the percentage uncertainty is around 1 per cent.

mcqs.q: A 200 g block of ice melts completely inside a sealed container. What is the mass of the water formed?
options: Less than 200 g, because some of the ice is used up in melting.
More than 200 g, because the water is denser than the ice was.
200 g at first, and then less as the water spreads itself out.
200 g, because exactly the same particles are still there.
mcqs.explain: Mass is conserved in a change of state; melting rearranges the particles but does not create or destroy any.

mcqs.q: Water is boiled away in an open pan standing on a balance, and the reading falls. Which statement is correct?
options: The steam has carried the mass out of the pan; none is lost.
The mass has been destroyed by the heat from the hotplate.
The water has become steam, and a gas has no mass at all.
The mass has been turned into the energy needed for boiling.
mcqs.explain: Mass is conserved. The water molecules are now in the air, so they are no longer on the balance.

mcqs.q: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
options: Steam is a new substance, but the water can be made again.
Reversing it is possible, and chemical changes are never reversible.
Cooling the steam gives back water with its original properties.
No energy at all is transferred to the water while it boils.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's test: the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

mcqs.q: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls. Which explanation is correct?
options: The solid has been used up, so that mass no longer exists.
The gas has left the dish, so the mass of it all is unchanged.
A chemical reaction has turned the solid into a new gas.
Sublimation skips the liquid state, so some mass is missed.
mcqs.explain: Sublimation is a change of state from solid straight to gas, and mass is conserved; the gas has simply left the balance.

mcqs.q: A 2 kg block of aluminium is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?
options: Half, because each piece now has only half of the mass.
The same, because the mass and the volume both halve.
Half, because each piece is lighter than the whole block.
Double, because the volume of each piece has been halved.
mcqs.explain: Density is a property of the material. Halving m and V leaves the ratio m / V unchanged.
